content.title: About
content.content: Flax seeds are the edible seeds of the plant Linum usitatissimum, cultivated in temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. They have a mild nutty flavor with a slightly bitter note and a crunchy texture. Flax can be eaten raw, toasted, ground into flour, or added to baked goods, porridge, smoothies, and yogurts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Flax belongs to the Linaceae family and has been cultivated for over 5,000 years.
The seeds are a rich plant source of alpha‑linolenic acid (omega‑3), an essential polyunsaturated fatty acid.
Flax is used not only for food but also to produce flaxseed oil, fiber for textiles, and bio‑composites.
Seeds may be brown or golden, depending on the variety and processing method.
Flax plants produce bright yellow flowers that attract pollinators.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Flax seeds provide alpha‑linolenic acid, which supports heart and vascular health.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber from flax improves digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains lignans
items.content: Lignans have antioxidant properties and may positively influence hormonal balance.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Flax supplies vitamin E, magnesium, phosphorus, and calcium, supporting muscle and bone function.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: Ground flax is often used as a natural thickener and soothing agent in cooking.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to flax seeds.

items.title: Cyanogenic glycosides
items.content: Raw flax seeds contain small amounts of cyanogenic compounds; they should be consumed in moderation or lightly heated.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: High fiber content can affect the absorption of certain drugs; separate intake of medication and flax‑containing meals when needed.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Flax seeds can be eaten raw, sprinkled on yogurt, oatmeal, salads, added to smoothies, or baked into breads and cookies. Ground flax is commonly used as a thickener for sauces. For optimal absorption of healthy fats, it is recommended to grind the seeds before consumption.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store flax seeds in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent oil oxidation.
